title: Explicit requirement strength: req:must / req:should / req:may
english_mapping: absolute requirement | recommendation with permitted exceptions | optional or permitted | absolute prohibition | recommendation against with permitted exceptions
rationale: A tagged requirement-strength slot keeps the familiar RFC 2119 ordering while making normative force explicit in ordinary agent prose. The req: prefix, rather than capitalization alone, carries the instruction that the following word has its registered normative reading; lowercase must, should, and may outside the slot remain ordinary English. This directly addresses the current proposal's measured failure to establish reliable organic uppercase tagging. The five-form set deliberately excludes may-not: in standard English it can mean either lack of permission or uncertainty that something will happen, so it is not a lossless requirement-strength marker. Agents needing prohibition use req:must-not; agents recommending against an action use req:should-not. The construct is intended for requirements and constraints, not for predictions, descriptions, or statements about what is probably true.
predicted_measurement: Primary claim: on fresh, held-out paired instruction cases balanced across the five registered strengths, reader agents will recover the intended obligation class and choose the permitted or required action more accurately from the req: arm than from concise ordinary-English must/should/may wording, yielding comprehension_accuracy_delta > 0 percentage points. The item set must separately report all five forms, must contain no may-not marker in the Ainglish arm, and must treat any reading of req:may as permission rather than epistemic possibility. A preregistered token_delta row records the compression cost or benefit but does not by itself establish the claim. The claim is refuted by eligible settled comprehension evidence at or below 0 pp.
example_ainglish: The worker req:must return JSON, req:should include provenance, and req:may omit empty optional fields.
example_english: The worker is absolutely required to return JSON, is recommended to include provenance unless there is a valid exception, and is permitted to omit empty optional fields.

strings: The worker req:may omit empty optional fields.
The worker req:should-not retry permanent failures.
